title: UX and Human–Computer Interaction
description: How people see, remember and decide at a screen, and how to find out whether a design works for them. Covers research methods, usability heuristics, interaction design and accessibility to WCAG 2.2.
audience: A capable adult who uses software every day and has never studied why some interfaces work and others fail. They know basic proportions and percentages and have met the idea of a sample. No design or coding experience is needed; two lessons read short HTML snippets.
outcomes: You'll be able to explain why a screen is read the way it is, using grouping, attention and memory limits.
You'll be able to calculate pointing difficulty with Fitts's law and choice time with Hick's law, and say what each does not tell you.
You'll be able to choose a research method (interview, survey, card sort, usability test, A/B test) for a given question, and spot a leading question.
You'll be able to judge an interface against Nielsen's ten heuristics and rate the severity of what you find.
You'll be able to check a colour pair, a touch target and a form against the relevant WCAG 2.2 success criteria.

modules.title: How people see, remember and act
modules.summary: The limits of perception, memory and movement that every layout works within.

modules.title: Finding out what users need
modules.summary: Interviews, surveys, card sorts, usability tests and experiments, and what each can and cannot show.

modules.title: Judging and shaping interactions
modules.summary: Heuristics, expert inspection, severity, and the details of forms, errors and feedback.

modules.title: Accessibility
modules.summary: WCAG 2.2 as a working checklist: contrast, keyboard, structure and target size.

lessons.title: How the eye groups a screen
lessons.objective: Use proximity, similarity, common region and alignment to predict which elements a viewer reads as one group.

concepts.title: Gestalt grouping
concepts.summary: Viewers perceive nearby, similar, enclosed or aligned elements as belonging together before they read any of them.

concepts.title: Visual hierarchy
concepts.summary: Size, contrast and position set the order in which a viewer's attention visits elements on a screen.

misconceptions: Learners think a divider line is needed to separate two groups; spacing alone usually does it, and the line adds noise.
Learners treat colour as decoration; colour similarity actually asserts that two things are alike, so reusing a colour for unrelated items misleads.
sequence: Show a form where every label sits equidistant between two fields and ask which field each label belongs to.
Name proximity: the gap decides, before anything is read. Wertheimer's 1923 paper described grouping by proximity and similarity.
Add similarity (colour, shape) and common region (a shared background), and show each overriding proximity in turn.
Alignment and continuity: a left edge reads as a column, a line of icons reads as a row.
Visual hierarchy: scan order follows size and contrast; squint at a page to see the hierarchy.
Conflicts: when proximity says one thing and colour another, the viewer hesitates.
examples: A form with labels 24 px above the field they name and 8 px below the previous field reads wrongly; moving the label to 4 px above its own field and 24 px below the previous one fixes it with no new element.
Two links styled blue and underlined, one of which is plain text, teach the viewer that blue underline means 'links', and then the plain text breaks the rule.

figures.shows: A mock sign-up form in two switchable views: labels equidistant between fields, and labels moved nearer their own fields. Dimensions labelled in px.
figures.learnerAction: Drag the label up or down and watch which field it joins.
figures.placement: Proximity as the first grouping cue.

figures.shows: Four small layouts of six dots, each with a different spacing, colour or enclosure pattern.
figures.learnerAction: Pick the layout that reads as three pairs.
figures.placement: Comparing proximity, similarity and common region.

questionPlan.sample: Two buttons sit 8 px apart, and a third sits 40 px from them. With no other cues, which reading is most likely?
choices: The first two form a group and the third stands apart
The last two form a group
questionPlan.answer: The first two form a group and the third stands apart

questionPlan.sample: A pale panel placed behind three related controls makes them read as one set. This is grouping by common ___.
A page uses red for error text and also for a decorative heading. What does the repeated colour tell the viewer?
choices: Nothing, because colour carries no meaning
The heading is more important than the error

historyNotes: Max Wertheimer published the grouping principles in 1923 (Untersuchungen zur Lehre von der Gestalt II).

lessons.title: What memory can hold
lessons.objective: Design to working-memory limits by chunking, and by letting users recognise instead of recall.

concepts.title: Working memory
concepts.summary: The small store that holds the items a person is using right now, estimated at roughly four chunks in recent work.

concepts.title: Chunking
concepts.summary: Grouping items into meaningful units so that more information fits in the same number of slots.

concepts.title: Recognition versus recall
concepts.summary: Picking an item from a visible set takes less memory than producing it from nothing.

misconceptions: Learners quote 'seven plus or minus two' as a design rule; Miller's 1956 figure was about span for items, and later estimates (Cowan, 2001) put working memory nearer four chunks.
Learners think a long menu is a memory problem; it is a search problem, and the memory problem is a user who must remember an option name they cannot see.
sequence: Ask the learner to read 0 7 7 0 0 9 0 0 1 2 3, look away, and write it down; then repeat grouped as 077 009 001 23.
Define working memory and chunk; give Miller 1956 and Cowan 2001 with the caution about the number.
Recognition versus recall: a command line against a menu; a password field against a saved-password prompt.
Design consequences: show state instead of asking users to remember it, keep related choices on one screen, and group long strings.
Cognitive load: extraneous load from layout versus the load the task itself carries.
examples: A 16-digit card number shown as four groups of four becomes four chunks instead of sixteen.
A checkout that asks the user to 'enter the code from the previous page' puts the code in memory; one that shows the code on the same page removes the load.

figures.shows: The same digit string drawn ungrouped and grouped, with chunk brackets over the grouped view.
figures.learnerAction: Toggle between the two views.

figures.shows: Pairs of tasks (recall vs recognition) for the same goal, such as typing a command versus choosing from a menu.
figures.learnerAction: none

questionPlan.sample: A phone number is displayed as 020 7946 0958. How many chunks does it have?
Which design relies on recognition rather than recall?
choices: Typing a country code from memory
Choosing a country from a dropdown list
questionPlan.answer: Choosing a country from a dropdown list

questionPlan.sample: Producing an answer with no cue at all is called ___.

historyNotes: George Miller's 'The Magical Number Seven, Plus or Minus Two' appeared in Psychological Review in 1956.
Nelson Cowan argued for about four chunks in Behavioral and Brain Sciences in 2001.

lessons.title: Distance, size and the number of choices
lessons.objective: Compute pointing difficulty with Fitts's law and decision time with Hick's law, and state what each leaves out.

concepts.title: Fitts's law
concepts.summary: Time to reach a target grows with the index of difficulty ID = log2(D/W + 1), where D is distance to the target and W its width along the line of motion (Shannon formulation).

concepts.title: Hick's law
concepts.summary: For n equally likely choices the decision time grows as b·log2(n + 1).

concepts.title: Response-time limits
concepts.summary: About 0.1 s feels instant, 1 s keeps the flow of thought, and 10 s is the limit of attention on a task.

misconceptions: Learners read Hick's law as 'fewer items is always better'; it says time grows slowly with log n, and a well-organised long list can beat a deep tree of menus.
Learners think a bigger target helps only a little; because W is in the denominator, doubling the width cuts the ID by the same drop as halving the distance.
sequence: Paul Fitts's 1954 tapping experiments: faster for wider, nearer targets; speed traded against accuracy.
State ID = log2(D/W + 1) in bits and compute three cases with D and W.
Consequences: screen edges and corners behave as if infinitely wide in the direction of travel; big primary buttons; destructive buttons placed away from frequent ones.
Hick–Hyman: decision time against log2(n+1); compute n = 7 and n = 15.
What the laws leave out: familiarity, labels, grouping; Hick's law needs equally likely options.
Response-time limits from Miller 1968 and Nielsen: 0.1 s, 1 s, 10 s.
examples: D = 7 cm, W = 1 cm gives ID = log2(8) = 3 bits. Widen the target to 2 cm and ID = log2(4.5) = 2.17 bits.
A menu of 7 equally likely items gives log2(8) = 3; 15 items give log2(16) = 4, so doubling the list adds one unit of b, not double.

figures.shows: ID against D/W for the Shannon form, with points for the worked examples.
figures.learnerAction: Move sliders for D and W and read ID.

figures.shows: A machine taking n and giving log2(n+1).
figures.learnerAction: Enter n and read the output.

questionPlan.sample: A target is 1 cm wide and 15 cm away. What is ID = log2(D/W + 1), in bits?
A target is 2 cm wide and 6 cm away. What is ID in bits?
A menu has 15 equally likely items. What is log2(n + 1)?
Why is a button at the screen's top edge easy to hit with a mouse?
choices: The pointer stops at the edge, so the target is effectively very tall
The target is closer to the keyboard
questionPlan.answer: The pointer stops at the edge, so the target is effectively very tall

historyNotes: Paul Fitts published his tapping experiments in 1954; MacKenzie's 1992 paper popularised the Shannon form log2(D/W + 1) in HCI.
William Hick (1952) and Ray Hyman (1953) reported the log relation between choices and reaction time.

lessons.title: Mental models and the two gulfs
lessons.objective: Use Norman's terms to say why a user could not work out how to act, or could not tell what happened.

concepts.title: Mental model
concepts.summary: A person's working picture of how a system behaves, which may differ from how it is built.

concepts.title: Signifier
concepts.summary: A perceivable cue that shows where and how an action can be taken.

concepts.title: Gulf of execution
concepts.summary: The gap between what a user wants to do and the actions the system makes available and visible.

concepts.title: Gulf of evaluation
concepts.summary: The gap between the system's state and the user's ability to perceive and interpret it.

misconceptions: Learners use 'affordance' for any visible cue; an affordance is what the object allows, and the visible cue is the signifier.
Learners blame the user for an unclear screen; both gulfs are properties of the design.
sequence: A door with a flat plate and a door with a handle: which needs a 'push' sign, and why.
Mental model versus conceptual model of the designer, and the system image as the only channel between them.
Affordance (Gibson, 1979) and signifier (Norman's later term).
The two gulfs and the loop of goal, plan, act, perceive, interpret, compare.
Bridging the gulfs: constraints, mapping, feedback.
examples: A thermostat that shows only the target temperature leaves the user unable to tell whether the heating is running: a gulf of evaluation.
An icon-only toolbar with no labels: the user wants to export but cannot find the action: a gulf of execution.

figures.shows: A loop diagram: user goal, plan, act, system, perceive, interpret, compare, with the two gulfs drawn as gaps on either side of the system.
figures.learnerAction: Select a case and see where the loop breaks.

questionPlan.sample: A user taps 'Save', and nothing on screen changes. Which gulf is this?
A cue that shows where an action can be taken, such as a button's raised edge, is called a ___.
A user cannot find which menu holds 'Export'. Which gulf is this?

historyNotes: James Gibson coined 'affordance' in 1979; Norman adopted it in 1988 and introduced 'signifier' in the 2013 revised edition.

lessons.title: Asking people: interviews and surveys
lessons.objective: Choose between an interview and a survey, write a non-leading question, and read a survey's margin of error.

concepts.title: Leading question
concepts.summary: A question whose wording suggests the answer wanted.

concepts.title: Margin of error
concepts.summary: For a proportion p from n independent responses, 95% margin = 1.96·sqrt(p(1−p)/n).

concepts.title: Say versus do
concepts.summary: What people report about their behaviour often differs from what they do.

misconceptions: Learners believe a larger survey fixes a biased sample; margin of error shrinks with n, bias does not.
Learners believe interviews should ask users what features they want; users are better at describing past behaviour than proposing solutions.
sequence: Two versions of one question ('How much do you like the new search?' against 'How did you find the last thing you looked for?').
Interviews: open questions, past behaviour, follow-ups; surveys: closed questions, scale, scale.
Bias sources: leading wording, social desirability, self-selected respondents.
Margin of error formula and a worked case at n = 100 and n = 400.
Matching method to question: why (interview), how many (survey), what do they do (observation).
examples: With p = 0.5 and n = 100, the margin is 1.96 × sqrt(0.25/100) = 1.96 × 0.05 = 0.098, about 9.8 percentage points.
At n = 400 the margin is 1.96 × 0.025 = 0.049, about 4.9 points: four times the sample halves the margin.

figures.shows: A bar of survey results with an error band that changes with n.
figures.learnerAction: Slide n from 25 to 1600 and watch the band narrow.

figures.shows: Three question wordings next to the bias each one adds.
figures.learnerAction: none

questionPlan.sample: A survey of n = 400 gives p = 0.5. What is the 95% margin of error in percentage points, to one decimal place? (1.96·sqrt(p(1−p)/n))
Which question is not leading?
choices: Don't you agree the new menu is easier?
How would you describe finding a setting last week?
How much did you love the redesign?
questionPlan.answer: How would you describe finding a setting last week?

questionPlan.sample: Quadrupling the sample size changes the margin of error by what factor?

lessons.title: Sorting content and testing where things are
lessons.objective: Plan an open card sort and a tree test, and calculate how many items a menu structure can reach.

concepts.title: Card sort
concepts.summary: Participants group content items into categories, showing the structure they expect.

concepts.title: Tree test
concepts.summary: Participants find items in a text-only hierarchy, measuring whether the structure and labels work.

concepts.title: Breadth and depth
concepts.summary: A hierarchy with b choices per level and d levels can reach b^d items.

misconceptions: Learners think a card sort tests a navigation; it generates structure ideas, and a tree test is what checks a structure.
Learners always choose the shallowest menu; deep menus with clear labels can outperform a wide one with vague labels.
sequence: Information architecture: organisation, labelling, navigation and search as four systems.
Open card sort versus closed card sort.
Tree testing: tasks, success rate and directness.
b^d reach and the breadth-versus-depth trade-off.
Labels: user words against internal words.
examples: 12 choices per level and 3 levels reach 12^3 = 1,728 items. Eight per level over 3 levels reach 512.
A tree test: 20 of 25 participants reach the correct leaf, 80% success.

figures.shows: Cards for a store's products to be grouped into a draggable layout.
figures.learnerAction: Drag cards into groups and name them.

figures.shows: A three-level tree with b children per node, switchable between b = 4 and b = 8.
figures.learnerAction: Switch b and count leaves.

questionPlan.sample: A menu has 8 choices per level over 3 levels. How many items can it reach?
You have a proposed site structure and want to know if people can find items in it. Which method?
In a tree test 18 of 24 participants reach the correct leaf. What is the success rate, as a percentage?

historyNotes: Peter Morville and Louis Rosenfeld's book Information Architecture for the World Wide Web (1998) set out the four systems.

lessons.title: Watching people use it
lessons.objective: Plan a think-aloud usability test, compute a task success rate and a SUS score, and explain why testing repeats in small rounds.

concepts.title: Think-aloud protocol
concepts.summary: Participants speak their thoughts while they work on a task, revealing what they notice and expect.

concepts.title: Problem discovery model
concepts.summary: With a per-user detection rate L, n users find a proportion 1 − (1 − L)^n of the problems; Nielsen and Landauer's average L was about 0.31.

concepts.title: System Usability Scale
concepts.summary: Ten five-point items scored (odd items: response − 1; even items: 5 − response), summed and multiplied by 2.5, range 0 to 100.

misconceptions: Learners hear 'five users is enough' as a total sample; the claim was that five per round finds most problems for one group of users, and the plan is to fix and retest.
Learners treat SUS as a percentage; it is a score on a 0 to 100 scale and 68 is about the historical average.
sequence: A scenario-based task ('You want to change your delivery date') against a task naming the interface ('Click Orders').
The facilitator's role: observe, do not help, probe after.
Metrics: success, time, errors, satisfaction.
Discovery formula and worked case at n = 5.
SUS scoring from ten responses.
Moderated versus unmoderated, in person versus remote.
examples: A participant answers 4 on all odd items and 2 on all even items: odd items give 3 each (15), even items give 3 each (15), 30 × 2.5 = 75.

figures.shows: 1 − (1 − L)^n against n, for L = 0.31 and L = 0.15.
figures.learnerAction: Move n and L.

figures.shows: A SUS answer sheet with ten items and a participant's responses, with a working column to fill.
figures.learnerAction: Fill the working column.

questionPlan.sample: With L = 0.31, what percentage of problems do 5 users find, to the nearest whole number? (1 − 0.69^5)
A participant gives 4 to every odd-numbered SUS item and 2 to every even-numbered item. What is the SUS score?
Which task is better written for a usability test?
choices: Click the 'Orders' tab and change the date.
Your parcel is arriving on a day you will be away; get it delivered a day later.
Tell us if the date picker is clear.
questionPlan.answer: Your parcel is arriving on a day you will be away; get it delivered a day later.

historyNotes: Nielsen and Landauer published the problem discovery model in 1993 (INTERCHI '93).

lessons.title: Experiments and analytics
lessons.objective: Judge whether an A/B result is distinguishable from chance, and say what analytics cannot explain.

concepts.title: A/B test
concepts.summary: Randomly assign users to two versions and compare a metric.

concepts.title: Two-proportion z
concepts.summary: z = (p2 − p1) / sqrt(p1(1−p1)/n1 + p2(1−p2)/n2); at the 95% level |z| must exceed 1.96.

concepts.title: The why gap
concepts.summary: Analytics show what users did, and give no reason.

misconceptions: Learners treat any difference as a win; 4.0% against 4.8% with 1,000 users each is not distinguishable from chance.
Learners stop a test the moment the result looks good, which inflates false positives.
sequence: Why random assignment matters.
Worked difference between two conversion rates.
Sample size set in advance; not peeking.
Qualitative follow-up for 'why'.

figures.shows: Two sampling distributions of conversion rate whose overlap changes with n.
figures.learnerAction: Raise n and watch the distributions separate.

questionPlan.sample: Version B converts at 4.8% and A at 4.0%, each with 1,000 users, and z ≈ 0.87. At the 95% level this result is:
If the standard error of the difference is 0.01 and the observed difference is 0.02, what is z?
Analytics show 60% of users abandon at step 3. What can you conclude?

lessons.title: Ten usability heuristics
lessons.objective: Name Nielsen's ten heuristics and assign a described problem to the one it violates.

concepts.title: Usability heuristic
concepts.summary: A broad rule of thumb for judging an interface, derived from patterns in found problems.

concepts.title: Nielsen's ten heuristics
concepts.summary: Visibility of system status; match between system and real world; user control and freedom; consistency and standards; error prevention; recognition rather than recall; flexibility and efficiency of use; aesthetic and minimalist design; help users recognise, diagnose and recover from errors; help and documentation.

misconceptions: Learners treat the heuristics as laws; they are rules of thumb to prompt questions.
Learners map each problem to a single heuristic; several can apply, and the evaluator should note the one that explains the most.
sequence: Nielsen and Molich's 1990 origin, refined by Nielsen in 1994 from factor analysis of 249 usability problems (verify).
Walk through all ten with one screen per heuristic.
Then classify short problem statements.
Where two heuristics overlap, pick the more explanatory.
examples: A 20-second upload with no progress indicator violates visibility of system status.
'Error 0x80070057' shown as the only message violates both match with the real world and help recognising errors.

figures.shows: Five annotated screenshots (drawn as SVG), each with a visible defect.
figures.learnerAction: Choose the violated heuristic for each.

questionPlan.sample: How many heuristics are in Nielsen's list?
A form deletes a record immediately with no undo. Which heuristic does this violate?
A spinner runs for 20 seconds with no message. Which heuristic?

historyNotes: Nielsen and Molich presented heuristic evaluation in 1990; Nielsen's 1994 list of ten is still the one in common use.

lessons.title: Inspecting an interface and rating what you find
lessons.objective: Run a heuristic evaluation, rate the severity of each problem on a 0–4 scale, and compare it with a cognitive walkthrough.

concepts.title: Heuristic evaluation
concepts.summary: Several evaluators independently inspect an interface against heuristics and then merge their findings.

concepts.title: Severity rating
concepts.summary: A 0–4 scale, from not a problem to usability catastrophe, based on frequency, impact and persistence.

concepts.title: Cognitive walkthrough
concepts.summary: An evaluator steps through a task asking, at each action, whether the user will try it, notice it, connect it to the goal and see progress.

misconceptions: Learners think evaluators should agree before they inspect; independent inspection first is what makes the merge useful.
Learners think inspection replaces testing; it finds different problems, and experts miss problems real users hit.
sequence: Inspection versus testing.
How the evaluation runs: individual passes, then merge.
Why more evaluators: each finds only part. If one finds 35% independently, three together reach 1 − 0.65^3.
Severity: frequency, impact, persistence; 0 to 4.
Cognitive walkthrough's four questions.
examples: Three independent evaluators each finding 35% of problems: 1 − 0.65^3 = 1 − 0.2746 = 0.7254, about 72.5% (an upper bound, since evaluators overlap).
A mislabelled button that every user hits on every visit and cannot avoid scores higher than a typo on a settings page.

figures.shows: A findings log with columns for screen, problem, heuristic, severity 0–4.
figures.learnerAction: Fill the severity column for given problems.

figures.shows: Cumulative share of problems found against number of evaluators.
figures.learnerAction: none

questionPlan.sample: If each evaluator independently finds 35% of problems, what percentage do 3 find together, to one decimal place? (1 − 0.65^3)
A problem that stops users from completing checkout. On Nielsen's 0–4 scale, it is:
You have no users available this week and a mock-up. Which method fits?

lessons.title: Forms, errors and feedback
lessons.objective: Design a form field and its error message so that the user can see what went wrong and how to put it right.

concepts.title: Error prevention
concepts.summary: Design that makes the error impossible or unlikely, such as constraints, defaults and reversible actions.

concepts.title: Anatomy of an error message
concepts.summary: A good error message says what happened, why, and what to do next, in the user's words, next to the field.

concepts.title: Undo over confirmation
concepts.summary: Allowing a reversal is usually better than asking 'Are you sure?', which users answer by habit.

misconceptions: Learners believe confirmation dialogs prevent mistakes; people click through them by habit, and undo works better for reversible actions.
Learners validate only on submit; inline validation after leaving a field avoids a wall of errors, but should not fire while the user is still typing.
sequence: Slips and mistakes (Norman, Reason).
Prevention: constraints, defaults, formatting help.
Error message anatomy.
Undo versus confirm.
Labels, placeholders (not a replacement for labels), and the HTML that supports them (type, required, autocomplete).
Link to WCAG 3.3.1 error identification and 3.3.7 redundant entry.
examples: Weak: 'Invalid input.' Better: 'The email address is missing an @. Enter it like name@example.com.'
A date field with a calendar picker removes the format error entirely.

figures.shows: A sign-up form with three error states drawn as switchable views: top-of-page summary, inline error, and no error.
figures.learnerAction: Switch views and rate each for clarity.

questionPlan.sample: Which message follows good error-message practice?
choices: The card number needs 16 digits; you entered 15.
questionPlan.answer: The card number needs 16 digits; you entered 15.

questionPlan.sample: Letting users reverse an action instead of asking them to confirm it is called providing ___.
In <input type="email" required>, which two things does the browser check before submitting?
questionPlan.answer: That the field is not empty and that its value looks like an email address

lessons.title: WCAG and contrast
lessons.objective: Explain the structure of WCAG 2.2 and compute whether a colour pair meets the contrast criteria.

concepts.title: POUR
concepts.summary: WCAG organises requirements under four principles: Perceivable, Operable, Understandable, Robust.

concepts.title: Conformance levels
concepts.summary: Success criteria are levelled A, AA and AAA; AA is the usual legal and policy target.

concepts.title: Contrast ratio
concepts.summary: (L1 + 0.05) / (L2 + 0.05), where L1 is the lighter colour's relative luminance; AA needs 4.5:1 for normal text, 3:1 for large text and for key interface components (1.4.3, 1.4.11).

misconceptions: Learners think accessibility is for a small group; it covers permanent, temporary and situational limits (bright sun, a broken arm, a noisy room).
Learners think any grey that looks readable passes; #777777 on white gives 4.48:1 and fails 4.5:1, while #767676 gives 4.54:1 and passes.
sequence: WCAG 2.0 (2008), 2.1 (2018), 2.2 (October 2023), each building on the last; 4.1.1 Parsing was removed as obsolete in 2.2.
POUR with one criterion under each.
Levels, and what conformance claims mean.
Contrast ratio: formula with worked luminance values.
Large text (18 pt, or 14 pt bold) and non-text contrast.
Never use colour alone (1.4.1).
examples: Black on white: (1 + 0.05) / (0 + 0.05) = 21:1, the maximum.
L1 = 0.5 and L2 = 0.05: 0.55 / 0.10 = 5.5:1, which passes AA for normal text.

figures.shows: A contrast calculator taking two luminance values.
figures.learnerAction: Enter L1 and L2 and read the ratio.

figures.shows: Sample text swatches with ratios hidden until the learner commits a pass/fail judgment (never beside the question).
figures.learnerAction: Mark each swatch pass or fail.

questionPlan.sample: Two colours have relative luminance 0.5 and 0.05. What is the contrast ratio (the lighter divided as (L1+0.05)/(L2+0.05))?
Normal-size text has a contrast ratio of 4.48:1. Does it meet WCAG 2.2 AA (1.4.3)?
In POUR, the R stands for ___.

historyNotes: WCAG 2.2 became a W3C Recommendation on 5 October 2023 (verify).

lessons.title: Keyboard, structure and target size
lessons.objective: Check an interface for keyboard operation, correct semantic elements, text alternatives and minimum target size.

concepts.title: Keyboard operability
concepts.summary: Every function works from a keyboard (2.1.1), focus is visible (2.4.7) and not hidden behind other content (2.4.11).

concepts.title: Semantic markup
concepts.summary: Native elements such as button, label, and headings give assistive technology a name, role and state without extra code (4.1.2).

concepts.title: Target size minimum
concepts.summary: Pointer targets must be at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels, or have enough spacing (2.5.8, AA, new in WCAG 2.2).

misconceptions: Learners think a div with a click handler is equivalent to a button; it is not focusable, has no role and ignores Enter and Space unless these are added.
Learners add alt text to every image; decorative images should have an empty alt so screen readers skip them.
sequence: Unplug the mouse: tab through a page and note where focus goes.
Native elements against div with onclick.
Alt text: informative, functional, decorative.
Headings as a document outline; labels tied to inputs.
Target size: 24 CSS px minimum at AA; 44 CSS px at AAA (2.5.5).
Reflow at 320 CSS px (1.4.10) and resize to 200% (1.4.4).

questionPlan.sample: Which element is focusable and operable by Enter and Space by default?
What is the minimum target width, in CSS pixels, under WCAG 2.2 SC 2.5.8 (AA)?
A purely decorative divider image should have which alt attribute?

courseCheck: A mixed check: grouping and hierarchy on a screen; chunk counts; Fitts's ID and Hick's log; classifying a gulf; choosing a research method for a stated question; margin of error and the two-proportion z; the discovery formula and SUS scoring; mapping a defect to a heuristic with a severity; writing an error message; computing a contrast ratio; and a short audit of HTML for keyboard, labels, alt and target size.
platformNeeds: A contrast checker figure: two colour pickers with live luminance and ratio (fallback: number_machine with luminance values).
A fixed-wording hotspot figure for marking defects on a mock-up screen (fallback: diagram_choice with SVG screens).
An HTML snippet code-reading question type that renders the markup next to the question and shows tab order.
A Fitts's-law tapping trial the learner can perform with timing.
unverified: No external source could be opened in this session (the network blocked w3.org, nngroup.com and others), so every source has verified: false and the writer must open them before citing section numbers.
WCAG 2.2 criterion numbers and levels (1.4.3, 1.4.11, 2.4.11, 2.5.8, 2.5.5, 3.3.7), the 24 CSS px target size and the 5 October 2023 date are from memory.
#767676 = 4.54:1 and #777777 = 4.48:1 on white are widely cited and should be recomputed with the WCAG relative luminance formula.
Nielsen's 35% single-evaluator figure, the 249 problems in the 1994 factor analysis, and L = 0.31 from Nielsen and Landauer 1993 are from memory.
The Shannon form of Fitts's law is given with MacKenzie 1992 as its source; the original 1954 formula used 2D/W.
Cowan 2001 and Miller 1956 dates are from memory.
